items.title: The Telemetry Lie
items.stakes: Valmera's training rooms go dark for eight minutes every hour. The dashboard says they never have.
items.clock: Before Monday's new intake in Valmera.
items.reward: Rooms that stay up — and a monitor that could have told you if they didn't.

objectives.text: Find what the monitor can't see
Decide how the schedule is fixed
Decide what the monitor must see

items.rumor: A hundred percent of the moments we looked.

items.alt: Valmera's training centre, room 4: a class at desks, the front display dark. Luis points at it; Maya, visiting, stares.
items.caption: Back at ten-thirteen. Every hour.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #66 · AVERY'S LENS  Only report what you could have seen  A dashboard must say how it looks, not just what it saw — an outage between two samples is not uptime.  The training rooms died for eight minutes every hour; the dashboard, sampling every fifteen on the quarter hour, reported 100% for a month.

items.alt: At HQ, the estate dashboard on the wall: Valmera Training, 30-day uptime 100.0%, incidents 0. Henrik on the phone in front of it.

bubbles.text: The dashboard says a hundred percent. Close Luis's tickets.

items.caption: Two truths. One of them is sampling.

items.prompt: 11:00. Henrik says close the tickets; Luis says his rooms are useless. What do you do?
unknown: Why the monitor can't see it
items.risk: A new intake taught in rooms that vanish every hour.
timeout: The tickets are closed on the dashboard's word.

hints.text: When does it happen — and when does the monitor look?

options.label: Close them — the dashboard says 100%
options.result: Luis stops raising tickets. The rooms keep dying.
options.consequence: Believed the sampler over the people in the room.
options.fail: A monitor can only report what it looks at.

options.label: Line up the complaint times against the clock, read the codecs' own logs, and check exactly when the monitor polls
options.result: Complaints at :05; restarts at :05; polls at :00 and :15.
options.consequence: Three records that explain each other.

options.label: Send someone to sit in a room all week
options.result: They see it — slowly — and can't say why.

items.title: Between the samples.
items.body: The monitor polls every room every fifteen minutes, aligned to the clock: :00, :15, :30, :45. The rooms are down from :05 to :13. Every poll lands just before or just after. Even if the polls fell at random, a fifteen-minute poll would catch an eight-minute outage only about half the time — 8 ÷ 15. Phase-locked, it catches none.
items.label: Test: how many outages does the monitor see — and what's the real availability?

items.alt: A timeline from 9:00 to 10:30: red outages from 9:05 to 9:13 and 10:05 to 10:13; blue poll ticks at every quarter hour, each landing before or after the red. Dashboard 100%, real class-hour availability about 87%.
items.caption: Every poll just misses.

items.prompt: Every tool HQ gives me says my rooms are perfect. My teachers say they're useless. Who do you believe?

options.label: “The teachers — and then I make the tools able to see what the teachers see.”
options.reply: That's the first HQ answer I've liked this year.

options.label: “The data, usually.”
options.reply: Your data looked at my rooms four times an hour. My teachers are in them all day.

options.label: “Both — let's put the complaint times beside the logs.”
options.reply: Fine. Bring coffee. It's a long log.

items.title: interval: 900 s
items.body: The estate monitoring profile: ‘interval 900 s, aligned to the clock’. Aligned, so the graphs look tidy. Aligned, so every poll lands at :00, :15, :30 and :45 — for ever.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Luis beside a board. Your rooms die for eight minutes at five past every hour. We poll every fifteen, on the quarter hour. What does the dashboard see? Nothing. Every poll lands at :00 or :15; the outage sits between them. Even at random times it'd only catch… eight in fifteen. About half. So the requirement isn't ‘poll more’. It's ‘see any outage of five minutes or more’ — and that sets the interval.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Polling interval   Event-driven monitoring   Cron schedule   Heartbeat check   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Catching an outage by polling   ƒ FORMULA · Catching an outage by polling  P = min(1, d ÷ T)   P  chance one outage is seen, if polls fall at random times  d  outage length  T  polling interval, same units as d      ƒ Ask for the formula · Rate   ƒ FORMULA · Rate  rate = count ÷ time   count  how many events  time  over how long

items.label: **Learn it now:** sampling, polling and scheduled jobs.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · tap a plate to open it full size     The five fundamentals of sound     Sound, rooms and signals — five views     Point it at people, not at the ceiling

items.title: Nyquist, Shannon and the space between samples
items.body: In 1928 Harry Nyquist worked out how many independent pulses a telegraph line of a given bandwidth can carry. In 1949 Claude Shannon set the idea down as the sampling theorem: sample often enough, or lose what happens between the samples. A monitor that polls is a sampler too — and an outage shorter than its interval is a signal it can't see.

items.title: Five past every hour.
items.body: The rooms' nightly reset — clear stuck calls, reload the panel — was meant for 02:05. Its schedule reads ‘5 * * * *’: minute five of every hour. The deployment template's hour field was marked optional; left blank, it became a wildcard. Sixty Harrowmere rooms are queued from the same template next month.
items.label: Test: read the schedule — and find where it came from.

items.alt: The reset task's schedule in large monospace: ‘5 * * * *’ in red, meaning five past every hour; the template form's hour field left blank; 18 Valmera rooms affected and 60 Harrowmere rooms queued.
items.caption: One blank field.

items.title: Hour: (optional)
items.body: The deployment form for template TR-3: ‘Nightly reset — Minute: 5 · Hour: (optional)’. Left blank, ‘optional’ becomes ‘every’. Sixty Harrowmere rooms are queued from it for next month.

items.prompt: 14:30 Valmera. Classes run until 18:00. How is the schedule fixed?
items.risk: Sixty more rooms dying every hour next month.
timeout: The Harrowmere rollout starts on schedule.

hints.text: Whose window — and where did the typo come from?

options.label: Delete the reset task everywhere, now
options.result: The nightly reset had a job: clearing stuck calls. By Thursday two rooms hang.
options.consequence: Removes a design to remove a typo.

options.label: In Luis's 19:00 change window: ‘5 2 * * *’ in the 18 rooms and in the template, the hour field made required — and the 60 queued Harrowmere rooms held until then
options.result: Applied at 19:10. Wednesday's classes run clean. The Harrowmere rollout waits a week.
options.consequence: His rooms in his window; your template fixed at the source.

options.label: Change the monitor to poll every minute instead
options.result: 36,000 polls an hour — three times the server's budget — and the rooms still restart.
options.consequence: Better eyes on an unfixed fault.

options.label: Ask teachers to start lessons at quarter past
options.result: They lose fifteen minutes to save eight.
options.consequence: A workaround that costs more than the fault.

items.label: **Work it out:** see every outage that matters.

items.alt: Wednesday in room 4: the display bright at 11:05; Luis gestures at the wall clock; Maya smiles.

bubbles.text: And if it isn't, we'll know before your teacher does.

items.prompt: Thursday. What must the estate monitor be able to see?
items.risk: The next eight-minute fault, invisible again.
timeout: The next short outage is found by a teacher.

hints.text: What's the shortest outage that matters — and what does that make T?

options.label: Everything — poll every minute
options.result: Three times the server's budget; the platform team says no.

options.label: Requirement: any outage of five minutes or more. Poll every five minutes (7,200 an hour, inside the 12,000 budget), take restart events from the codecs as they happen, and run test calls into a sample of rooms in class hours
options.result: A test pull of one room's network shows red within five minutes; a restart shows within seconds.
options.consequence: A requirement first, then the means — polls, events and outcomes.

options.label: Keep fifteen minutes — users will complain if something's wrong
options.result: They did, for a month, and were told the dashboard was green.
options.fail: A monitor that can't see the fault reassures nobody.

options.label: Monitor only the rooms that complain
options.result: The next fault is in a room nobody's complained about yet.

One password. Seven hundred and forty doors.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Polling is sampling: P = min(1, d ÷ T), and if T ≤ d every outage is seen. Clock-aligned polls can miss a clock-aligned fault every time. Start from a requirement (“any outage of 5 minutes or more”), check the budget (devices × 60 ÷ T per hour), add event-driven alerts and an outcome check. And read the schedule: ‘5 * * * *’ is every hour.
